# Free Lunch Lab

> Free Lunch Lab ("There is such a thing as a free lunch.") is a curated directory of apps and projects that pay you a basic income or rewards just for existing: crypto UBI, passive apps, cashback and more. Every entry links to its official source and has a "last checked" month, and the risks and cautions are listed next to the rewards. The site is available in 7 languages (en, ja, zh, hi, es, de, ar).

- Referral links: some sign-up links are the maintainer's referral links. They are marked in the data (`referral` in services.json) and labelled "Referral link" below; official URLs are always given too.
- License: content is CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), referral links excluded.
- Data last checked: 2026-11
- Short index: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/llms.txt

### Circles (Gnosis App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/circles/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Sign-up: invite only (needs an invitation, code or approval from an existing member)
- Verification: Web of trust / invites
- Trust check: Cash out: Unverified; Market price: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://app.gnosis.io/

A Gnosis project where every person issues their own currency. Circles 2.0 launched in May 2025, and in June 2026 the Gnosis App was rebuilt around Circles. This site has no referral link for it yet

What you get: 1 CRC per hour (24 per day)

What you need: Sign up in the Gnosis App and get invited by an existing Circles member. The inviter pays 96 CRC and the newcomer gets 48 CRC as a welcome bonus

Cautions: You can’t start without a member to invite you. CRC’s market price and ways to cash out are not confirmed. Gnosis has announced plans to spin the Gnosis App out of Gnosis Ltd into a separate company, so details may change

### Mercari

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/mercari/
- Category: Cashback sites
- Payout: one-time
- Region: Japan only
- Verification: Phone number, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://jp.mercari.com/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://link.jp.mercari.com/70tO/lpthbfqe
- Referral code (maintainer's own): AJVWZX

Mercari’s friend invite for its flea-market app. Sign up with an invite code and both you and the inviter get ¥500 in points (within 14 days). Turn on “Point Investment”, launched on Sept 15, 2026, and free points you receive automatically buy Bitcoin or Ethereum

What you get: ¥500 in points (can be auto-converted into Bitcoin and more)

What you need: Japan residents. Enter the invite code on the sign-up screen (it can’t be added later). Point Investment needs ID verification and age 18 to 74 (sign-up from Japan confirmed in Oct 2026)

Cautions: Points expire 30 days after you get them (counting that day). Point Investment only uses free points granted after you turn it on. There is no fee, but prices include a spread, and crypto can fall in value. Points obtained improperly are cancelled

Tap a button in the app once every 24 hours to earn PI. The more people you refer, the faster you mine. Opened to the public in February 2025 and trades on OKX, Bitget, MEXC and others

What you get: PI every day

What you need: Sign up via the invite link (invite code: eltociear). To move your PI you need identity verification and migration to the mainnet wallet

Cautions: The price is down about 97% from its 2025 high of $2.99 (about $0.08 as of October 2026). Not listed on Binance, Coinbase or Japanese exchanges. Needs a daily tap, so it won’t build up if you leave it alone

### Mein Grundeinkommen

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/meingrundeinkommen/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.mein-grundeinkommen.de/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://meinbge.de/fuer-dich/4143ce95b90cf10386f4?utm_campaign=freundschaft

A free lottery run by a nonprofit association in Berlin and funded by crowdfunding donations. Draws are held regularly, and each winner gets €1,000 a month for 12 months, no strings attached (real cash, not crypto)

What you get: €1,000 a month for a year if you win

What you need: Register with your email and confirm your participation for each draw. You must be 16 or older, and your name and date of birth must match your ID if you win

Cautions: A 2020 statement from the organisation said anyone can take part regardless of age or where they live, but current rules for people outside Germany and payouts abroad are not confirmed. The site is in German. It's a lottery, so most entrants receive nothing. Winnings may be taxed in your country

### UBI4ALL

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/ubi4all/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.ubi4all.org/

A free raffle run by a German non-profit. Each time donations reach €9,600, a basic income worth €9,600 in total is raffled off, paid in cash with no strings attached. High-income countries such as Japan get €800 a month for 1 year, low-income countries €160 a month for 5 years. No referral bonus

What you get: €9,600 if you win (in Japan: €800 a month for a year)

What you need: Create a free account on the official site and register for each raffle (monthly donors from €1 are entered automatically). You must be 16 or older, and winners are verified with ID. Sign-up from Japan has not yet been tested by this site

Cautions: It’s a raffle, so the odds are low and depend on how many people take part. Raffles only happen when donations fill the €9,600 pot, so the timing is irregular. Unless you are a UBI Beaver, you have to register for each raffle. Residents of the previous winner’s country are excluded from the next draw. Payouts go to SEPA bank accounts; other methods have their fees taken from the prize. How the prize is taxed depends on your country

### Ğ1 (June)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/g1/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Sign-up: invite only (needs an invitation, code or approval from an existing member)
- Verification: Web of trust / invites
- Trust check: Cash out: With conditions; Market price: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://duniter.org/g1/

A libre currency based on the Relative Theory of Money. It runs on the open-source Duniter software, and every member receives newly created Ğ1 each day as a “Universal Dividend”. Launched in March 2017 and moved to Duniter v2 in March 2026. There is no referral link or referral bonus

What you get: Ğ1 every day once you are a member (Universal Dividend)

What you need: Create a wallet and get certified by at least 5 existing members through the Web of Trust. Certifiers are expected to know you in person

Cautions: The community is mostly French-speaking and built on in-person ties, so joining from outside it (e.g. from Japan) is very hard. Non-members can still hold Ğ1 in a wallet but do not receive the daily dividend. Ğ1 is mainly traded for goods and services, and swapping it for regular money is peer-to-peer only

### Palai

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/palai/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: Phone number
- Trust check: Cash out: No; Public operator: Unverified
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://palai.org/en
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://palai.org/en?referrer=eltociear%2B856536b6d-da3a-4f27-9bcf-8eef2ce05bc2

A currency that pays everyone a daily basic income just for being human. No app to install and nothing to pay. Unspent balances slowly “evaporate”, and that amount is redistributed as basic income. Refer a friend and you get one extra day of basic income

What you get: Palai (¶) basic income every day

What you need: Sign up via the referral link and get certified by adding a mobile phone number (no ID needed). You claim your income yourself; days not claimed within 10 days are lost

Cautions: As of Oct 2026 there is no way to cash Palai out into euros or other money and no official exchange rate; you can only trade it for goods and services with people who accept Palai. The site doesn’t name the operator, only that it is “supported by Social Impact Lab Leipzig”

### Dotare

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/dotare/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: not specified
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://dotare.io/

A global basic income fund on Cardano. Donated ADA is put to work through staking and similar, and the earnings are paid to recipients in ADA each month. For 2027 that is 10 ADA a month for 12 months. No income test. Run by Dotare, LLC in the US. No referral bonus

What you get: 10 ADA a month for a year if you are chosen (2027 cycle)

What you need: Be 18 or older. Sign up on the official site and apply for each year you want to take part. When your turn comes, pass a quick identity check (to show you are human) and set up a Cardano wallet to receive payments

Cautions: For the 2027 cycle, applications closed on 31 Aug 2026 and enrollment closes on 30 Nov 2026; when someone signing up now would start receiving is not confirmed. Payouts go in line order, and as of 24 Oct 2026 the site showed 147 citizens and 2 beneficiaries. ADA’s price swings a lot

A mini app inside World App that lets you claim the World Chain token ORO once a day. World’s listing says inviting friends earns more ORO, but as of Oct 2026 we found no invite link in the app. Developed by Grupo de Fiesta

What you get: ORO tokens every day

What you need: Install World App, prove you are human with World ID (confirmed from Japan with Orb verification), then open the ORO mini app and claim every day

Cautions: The daily amount is not stated officially. It is unknown whether a verification level below Orb is enough. ORO trades on DEXs but liquidity is small, and 1 ORO is worth less than ¥1 (Oct 2026). No company information about the operator could be found

### AXO (World App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/axo/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: World ID (Orb)

- Referral code (maintainer's own): 932BDA

A mini app inside World App: tap once a day to claim the World Chain token AXO. The “Premium” plan (1 WLD a month) triples the daily amount. There is also a referral system. The founder is David Mateos

What you get: AXO tokens every day

AXO can be swapped for WLD on a decentralized exchange (DEX), but as of Oct 2026 liquidity is only about $2,000 and one AXO is worth a tiny fraction of a cent. No operating company details were found

### AI-DAC (World App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/aidac/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: World ID (Orb)
- Trust check: Cash out: With conditions; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://lp.ai-dac.com/

A mini app inside World App that calls itself an “AI-powered universal basic income platform”. People verified as human with World ID receive DAC and use it to back autonomous “AI CEOs” that build apps, and to vote on releases. Run by its founder, Kei Iwami. No referral bonus

What you get: UBI in DAC tokens

What you need: Open the AI-DAC mini app in World App and prove you are human with World ID (confirmed from Japan with Orb verification)

Cautions: The amount, frequency and how to cash out are not stated officially. It is unknown whether a verification level below Orb is enough. DAC has no supply cap: the operator can mint more at any time, which can dilute its value. The official site says its value is not guaranteed, and DEX liquidity is tiny (Oct 2026)

### Ubiquitus

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/ubiquitus/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: US residents only, not available from Japan
- Verification: not specified
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.ubiquitus.org/

A US social experiment in a “basic income anyone can join”. Donations go into an invested fund, and each month 0.5% of it is split equally among all participants and paid via Venmo. Donating does not increase what you get. Founded by Ryan Frigo. No referral bonus

What you get: A small equal cash share on the 1st of each month (Venmo)

What you need: US residents aged 18+. Verify with a 1¢ Venmo transaction (no ID upload, no means test)

Cautions: As of Oct 2026 it cannot be used from Japan (the terms limit it to US residents; not working from Japan was confirmed first-hand). The per-person amount is tiny, falls with the pool, and payouts are stated to be not guaranteed and able to stop at any time. It describes itself as an informal social experiment, not a company. Recipients must report payments as income

### Gradido

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/gradido/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification
- Trust check: Cash out: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://gradido.net/en/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://gdd.gradido.net/u/eltociear

A currency system that calls itself a “natural economy”. Work for the common good earns an “active basic income” of 20 GDD an hour, up to 1,000 GDD a month. Unspent money shrinks at 50% a year. Run by Gradido Akademie in Austria

What you get: 20 GDD per hour of common-good work (up to 1,000 GDD a month)

What you need: Create a free Gradido account through the referral link, record your contributions to the common good and receive GDD (tested first-hand from Japan in Oct 2026)

Cautions: The official FAQ says it is for now a “gratitude points reward system”, not a cryptocurrency. There is no official way stated to exchange GDD for euros or other money. If someone you referred later contributes money (e.g. a donation), you receive GDT; signing up alone earns nothing

## Essays

### Does giving people money make them stop working? What the experiments found

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/does-cash-make-people-stop-working/
- Published: 2026-11-11

“Give people money for nothing and they’ll stop working.” It is the most common objection to basic income, and a fair question. It is also one that can be checked. For more than fifty years, governments, charities and researchers have handed out cash and measured what happened to work.

We lined up the main studies: the US negative income tax experiments of the 1970s, Canada’s Mincome, Alaska’s dividend, Iran’s national cash transfers, a reanalysis of seven government programmes in six countries, Finland, GiveDirectly’s long-term study in Kenya, Stockton, OpenResearch, and the 101 pilots in our table of US guaranteed income pilots (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/pilots/us/). Every figure comes from the papers and official reports, or from our earlier essays on OpenResearch (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/) and Finland (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/).

**Effect on work, by study**

| Study | When / where | Result | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SIME/DIME (negative income tax) | USA, 1970s | Worked less | Hours down 9–20% |
| Mincome | Canada, 1975–79 | Worked less | Hours down 1–3% |
| Alaska dividend | USA, since 1982 | No clear change | Part-time work up |
| Iran cash transfers | Since 2011 | No clear change | More work by women |
| Seven government programmes | Six countries | No clear change | No systematic effect |
| Finland | 2017–18 | No clear change | Year 2: +6 days |
| Kenya (GiveDirectly) | Since 2018 | No clear change | From wages to own business |
| Stockton (SEED) | 2019–21 | No clear change | Not significant |
| OpenResearch | USA, 2020–23 | Worked less | 1.3 hours a week less |
| US pilots with a control group | 17 evaluations | Worked less: 2, No clear change: 7, Worked more: 8 | Number of pilots |

Each dot is a study’s main result on work. The columns show direction, not size: the studies measure work in different units (hours, days, employment rates), so the sizes are in words. For the US pilots, the numbers count evaluations with a control group in each column; one more found people moving between kinds of work.

#### The evidence side by side

One distinction runs through everything below. “No significant effect” does not mean “no effect”. It means the gap between recipients and the control group was too small, given the noise in the data, to tell apart from chance. A small study can miss a real effect. A large one can rule out big effects but not small ones. Where a paper says what it can rule out, we say so.

| Program | Place and years | Payment | Design | Effect on work | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SIME/DIME (negative income tax) | Seattle and Denver, USA; from 1970, for 3 or 5 years | A guaranteed $3,800–$5,600 a year for a family of four (1971 dollars), reduced as other income rose | Randomised; about 4,800 families | Annual hours down about 9% for husbands, 20% for wives and 14% for single mothers (second year) | [9] |
| Mincome | Dauphin and Winnipeg, Canada; payments 1975–1979 | An income floor, reduced by 50 cents for each dollar of other income; anyone in Dauphin could claim it | Field experiment; the whole town of Dauphin was eligible | Hours down about 1% for men and 3% for married women | [10][11] |
| Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend | Alaska, USA; since 1982 | A yearly dividend for every resident: on average $1,495 per person (2010 dollars) | Alaska compared with a weighted mix of other states, 1977–2014 | No effect on employment; part-time work up 1.8 points (17%) | [8] |
| National cash transfers | Iran; from 2011 | Monthly deposits to more than 70 million people, worth 28% of median income per person | Panel data on when and how much households received (not randomised) | No reduction in hours or labour force participation; more work by women and self-employed men | [12] |
| Seven government cash transfer programmes | Honduras, Indonesia, Mexico (two), Morocco, Nicaragua, the Philippines | Cash for poor households | Reanalysis of 7 randomised trials | No systematic effect on whether, or how much, men or women worked | [13] |
| Basic income experiment | Finland; 2017–2018 | €560 a month for two years, tax-free | Randomised; 2,000 unemployed people vs other unemployed people | Year 1: 49.64 vs 49.25 days in work; year 2: about 6 more days | [5][6] |
| GiveDirectly long-term UBI | Siaya and Bomet, Kenya; from 2018, for 12 years | $0.75 a day per adult, paid monthly | Randomised by village: 44 villages (about 5,000 people) vs 100 control villages | Total hours unchanged; less wage work, more self-employment (after about two years) | [7] |
| SEED | Stockton, USA; 2019–2021 | $500 a month for two years | Randomised; 131 vs 200 | Differences in employment not significant | [2] |
| Unconditional Cash Study (OpenResearch) | Illinois and Texas, USA; 2020–2023 | $1,000 a month for three years | Randomised; 1,000 vs 2,000 who got $50 a month | About 1.3 fewer hours a week; 2.3 points less likely to be employed | [3][4] |
| 101 guaranteed income pilots | Across the USA; since 2018 | Median $500 a month | 18 evaluations with a control group report on work | 8 more work, 7 no clear difference, 2 less work, 1 a shift between kinds of work | [1] |

#### The 1970s: negative income tax and Mincome

Between 1968 and 1980 the US and Canadian governments ran five negative income tax experiments.[10] A negative income tax is not quite a basic income. It guarantees a minimum and then takes part of it back as other income rises, typically around 50 cents per dollar in these experiments. So they tested cash and a high tax on earnings at the same time.

The largest, in Seattle and Denver, enrolled about 4,800 families. Measured in the second year, husbands worked about 9% fewer hours than the control group, wives about 20% and single mothers about 14%.[9] Most of the husbands’ reduction came from longer unemployment, on average about 2.2 more weeks out of work; for wives and single mothers it was time out of the labour force.[9] Averaging the four US experiments, three reviews put the reduction for main earners at 5% to 7.9%. One of them, by Philip Robins (1985), found that “in no case is there evidence of a massive withdrawal from the labor force”.[10]

Canada’s Mincome, in Manitoba, made the town of Dauphin a “saturation site”: every resident could claim the guarantee. Families enrolled from late 1974, and payments ran until 1979.[11] Derek Hum and Wayne Simpson’s analysis of work (1993) found hours down about 1% for men and 3% for married women, smaller than in the US.[10] Mincome is better known for Evelyn Forget’s 2011 finding that hospitalisations in Dauphin fell by 8.5% relative to a comparison group; a 2021 reanalysis by David Green argues that, once earlier trends are taken into account, the data do not support that conclusion.[11]

#### Recent trials: Finland, Stockton and OpenResearch

Finland paid €560 a month, tax-free, to 2,000 randomly chosen unemployed people for two years. In the first year, recipients were in work for 49.64 days on average and the control group for 49.25: no effect.[5] Over roughly the second year, recipients worked about 6 days more. But a new “activation model” for the unemployed began that year and did not affect the two groups in the same way, so the second-year gap cannot all be credited to the basic income.[6] Our essay on Finland (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/) has the details.

Stockton’s SEED paid $500 a month for two years. A first-year report in 2021 said full-time work rose from 28% to 40% among recipients, and that figure is still widely quoted. The peer-reviewed analysis of the randomised trial (Journal of Urban Health, 2023; 131 recipients, 200 controls) found that the differences in employment were not statistically significant, before the pandemic or during it.[2]

OpenResearch’s study, backed by Sam Altman, is the largest and most carefully measured. 1,000 people aged 21 to 40 received $1,000 a month for three years; 2,000 received $50 a month. Recipients worked about 1.3 hours a week less than the control group, were 2.3 percentage points less likely to be employed, and earned about $1,900 a year less from work. The authors call it a 5 to 6% decline, “a moderate effect”.[3] Employment still rose in both groups, from 58% to 72% among recipients and from 59% to 74% in the control group.[4] Our essay on the study (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/) covers the rest.

#### 101 US pilots: what the evaluations say

Our table of US guaranteed income pilots (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/pilots/us/) lists 101 programmes; the median pays $500 a month. 53 have a published evaluation, and 34 of those compared recipients with a control or comparison group. 18 of the 34 report a result on work.[1]

Eight found more work than in the control group. In Oakland, full-time employment rose from 15% to 26% among recipients and from 14% to 18% in the control group; in Cambridge, Massachusetts, it rose from 36% to 40% while it fell from 30% to 28%. Arlington, Columbia, Durham and Denver reported similar results, and Baltimore’s recipients missed about 9 fewer hours of work a month. In Los Angeles County’s programme for young adults, employment rose 7 points, though the author credits much of that to the job training that came with the cash.[1]

Seven found no clear difference, Stockton among them. Two found less work: OpenResearch, and Compton, where labour force participation fell 13 points among people who had worked part-time, while full-time workers did not change. One, for artists in New York, found about 3.9 more hours a week on art and 2.4 fewer on other work.[1]

These are not 18 equal pieces of evidence. Many are short reports rather than peer-reviewed papers, samples are often 100 to 200 people, several give percentages without saying whether a difference is statistically significant, and some came with other services. The count shows the range of results, not a verdict. What it does not show is people dropping out of work.

#### Beyond rich countries: Kenya, Iran and seven programmes

GiveDirectly’s study in Kenya is the closest thing so far to a long-term basic income. In 44 villages, every adult receives $0.75 a day, paid monthly, for 12 years; 100 villages serve as controls, alongside villages paid for two years or in a lump sum.[7] After about two years, total household working hours had not fallen. The estimate was a small increase that was not significant, and the authors “can reject large decreases”. What changed was the kind of work: fewer hours of wage work in farming and more in non-farm self-employment, as people started or expanded small businesses. Wage workers from outside the villages filled the gap, and wages rose.[7]

Iran replaced energy subsidies with monthly cash deposits from 2011, reaching more than 70 million people and worth 28% of median income per person. Using differences in when households started receiving the money and how much it meant to them, Djavad Salehi-Isfahani and Mohammad Mostafavi-Dehzooei found “no evidence that cash transfers reduced labor supply”, and positive effects for women and self-employed men. In the working paper the exception was young people with weak ties to the labour market.[12]

Abhijit Banerjee, Rema Hanna, Gabriel Kreindler and Benjamin Olken went back to the data from seven randomised trials of government cash transfer programmes in Honduras, Indonesia, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua and the Philippines. They found “no systematic evidence that cash transfer programs discourage work”, for men or for women.[13] These programmes were aimed at poor households; they were not basic incomes.

#### Alaska: a payment to everyone, every year

Every Alaska resident has received a yearly dividend from the state’s Permanent Fund since 1982. The average was $1,495 per person in 2010 dollars, or about $3,900 for a family.[8] Damon Jones and Ioana Marinescu compared Alaska with a weighted mix of other states and found that the dividend “had no effect on employment” and raised part-time work by 1.8 percentage points (17%).[8]

They are careful about what that means. Their confidence intervals cannot rule out a positive effect on employment, so the extra part-time work may come from people moving from full-time to part-time, or from people joining the workforce part-time. Hours fell by less than one hour a week, and not significantly. Their explanation is that when everyone gets the money and spends it locally, demand for local services rises and offsets the pull towards working less; employment held up better in sectors serving local customers than in those trading with the rest of the world.[8]

#### Who worked less, and what they did instead

Where work fell, it fell for particular people. In the 1970s experiments it fell most for wives and single mothers, who worked fewer hours to begin with, so a few weeks off is a bigger percentage.[10] Husbands mostly took longer between jobs.[9] Young people cut their work by a large percentage but a small number of hours, and the official report notes that this did not come with more time in school.[9]

In OpenResearch, the drop was concentrated among people under 30, single parents and those with the highest household incomes at the start; for recipients over 30 there was no significant effect.[4] The hours went mostly to leisure. The paper rules out even small changes in time spent on childcare, job search or self-improvement, though spells without work lasted about 0.8 months longer.[3] In Kenya, people moved from wage work to their own businesses.[7] In Alaska, some moved to part-time work.[8] In Finland, Kela found that the basic income helped people who were already active, and did not solve the problems of those in the most difficult situations.[6]

Opinion: So the honest picture is not “nobody works less”. Some people do, by a few hours a week or a few weeks a year: mostly second earners and single parents, the young, and people between jobs. Whether that is a cost or the point depends on what you think that time is for.

#### Why a pilot is not a national basic income

Almost every study above differs from a real basic income in at least four ways.

How long it lasts. Most were temporary, and recipients knew when the money would stop. People may treat three years of cash differently from a payment for life. Alaska’s dividend is permanent but modest. Kenya’s 12-year group is the main test of a long commitment, and its published results cover the first two years.[7][8]

Who gets it. A pilot pays a few people in a place. A payment to everyone changes local demand, wages and prices: in Kenya wages rose as people left wage work, and in Alaska the effect on the local economy seems to have offset the individual one.[7][8] A pilot that pays a few hundred people cannot see this.

Who pays. In a pilot the money comes from outside. A national basic income has to be paid for, mostly through taxes, and higher taxes on earnings can themselves reduce work. The negative income tax experiments did take back about 50 cents per dollar earned, one reason their effects were larger; Finland’s experiment changed no taxes at all.[6][10] For what a basic income would cost, see our world map (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/basic-income-world-map/).

Who was studied. Most samples were people on low incomes, who respond more because the payment is large next to their earnings. A simulation for the Gary experiment estimated that a national programme would reduce work by about a third as much (1.6% rather than 4.5%).[10]

#### What we still do not know

No one has yet paid a permanent, universal basic income at a level people could live on, funded by taxes, and measured what happened to work. The evidence covers pieces of that: permanence with little money (Alaska), money without permanence (most pilots), everyone in a village (Kenya), and national scale with a targeted design (Iran, the seven programmes).

Many pilot results rest on self-reported surveys. Estimates also move as better data arrive: OpenResearch’s were revised upward in 2026 once state unemployment-insurance records were added.[3] And “no significant effect” from a study of 300 people is a far weaker claim than the same words from a study of 3,000.

#### What to take from it

Opinion: Across more than fifty years of experiments, in rich countries and poor ones, no study found that cash makes people stop working. Most found small reductions or none, and some found more work. Where work fell, it fell by hours a week or weeks a year, mostly for parents, the young and people between jobs.

Opinion: That is not the same as “basic income has no effect on work”. OpenResearch and the 1970s experiments measured real, if modest, reductions, and those numbers belong in any honest costing. The better question is not “will people stop working?” but “how much less, who, and is it worth it?” The data answer the first two parts. The third is a judgement for each of us.

### Which countries could afford a basic income tomorrow? A map of 211 countries

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/basic-income-world-map/
- Published: 2026-11-10

Pay every resident the World Bank’s international poverty line, $3.00 a day, for one year. In seven places that would cost less than 1% of GDP: Monaco (0.38%), Liechtenstein (0.50%), Luxembourg (0.74%), Bermuda (0.77%), Ireland (0.84%), Singapore (0.86%) and Macao (0.89%). In three it would cost more than the whole economy produces in a year: Burundi (115% of GDP), DR Congo (133%) and Somalia (163%).[1][8]

GDP is not what a government can spend, though. So for every country we also set the cost against the government’s own tax revenue. Of the 140 countries and territories with a recent figure, 24 could pay for it with less than a tenth of their tax revenue. 40 would need more than all of it.

[World map: World map: the yearly cost of paying everyone $3.00 a day, as a share of government tax revenue](https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/map/)

#### How the map is built

The cost is the population × $3.00 a day × 365 days: everyone, of every age, for one year. $3.00 is the World Bank’s international poverty line in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars, set in June 2025.[1] We convert it into local currency with the World Bank’s PPP conversion factor for household consumption, so that it buys roughly the same everywhere.[6] For 34 countries and territories without a usable factor we use the market exchange rate instead. Population and GDP are World Bank figures, with national statistics for seven featured countries; GDP is for 2025 in 186 of the 211.[2][3] The country shapes come from Natural Earth.[9]

Revenue is central government tax revenue as a share of GDP, from the World Bank.[4] We take the latest year, and only if it is no more than five years older than the GDP year. Where tax revenue is missing we would use total revenue instead,[5] but in this edition no country needed it. Of the 140 figures, 93 are for 2024, 19 for 2023, 8 for 2022, 9 for 2021 and 10 for 2020. Japan has no recent World Bank figure, so we use the tax and stamp revenue in its FY2026 national budget, ¥83.7 trillion.[7]

That leaves 71 countries and territories grey, home to 1.61 billion people: the World Bank has no tax figure for them since 2015, or only one more than five years old. They include Nigeria, Pakistan, Indonesia, Egypt, Vietnam, Iran, Qatar and Kuwait. Taiwan, North Korea, Eritrea, South Sudan and Yemen are not in the data at all. The full table, with every country’s figures and a link to its calculator page, is on the map page (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/map/).[8]

| Cost as a share of tax revenue | Countries and territories | People living there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 10% | 24 | 0.35 billion |
| 10–25% | 35 | 1.18 billion |
| 25–50% | 23 | 0.70 billion |
| 50–100% | 18 | 1.71 billion |
| Over 100% | 40 | 2.57 billion |
| No recent data | 71 | 1.61 billion |

#### Patterns by region and income

Europe stands out. Of the 48 countries in Europe and Central Asia with a figure, 41 come in under 25% of tax revenue and 18 under 10%. The lowest shares anywhere are Luxembourg (2.6%), Macao (3.2%), Denmark (4.4%), Norway (4.5%) and Ireland (4.7%). At the other end, 25 of the 32 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa with a figure would need more than their whole tax take; only Mauritius (18%) and Botswana (24%) come in under 25%.

Latin America sits in the middle: 10 of its 19 countries with a figure fall between 25% and 50%, among them Mexico (30%), Brazil (31%) and Colombia (34%). In South Asia all six countries have a figure and none is under 10%. The Maldives (24%) is lowest; India and Nepal (both 132%) and Bangladesh (160%) would need more than all their central tax revenue.

Income explains most of this. Grouping countries by GDP per person in US dollars, from the same data (this is not the World Bank’s income classification): among the 55 with a figure and more than $15,000 per person, the median cost is 11% of tax revenue and 49 are under 25%. Between $5,000 and $15,000 the median is 31%; between $1,500 and $5,000 it is 114%. Below $1,500, 17 of the 18 countries with a figure would need more than all their tax revenue, and the median is 287%.

Two things push in the same direction. Among the countries with a tax figure, a poverty line in PPP dollars is a bigger slice of the economy where incomes are low: the median cost is 1.9% of GDP above $15,000 per person and 36% below $1,500. And poorer governments collect a smaller share of GDP in tax: the median is 19.9% above $15,000 and 12.6% below $1,500.

#### Notable cases

Japan: ¥9,400 a month per person, about ¥13.9 trillion a year, or 2.1% of GDP. Against the ¥83.7 trillion of tax and stamp revenue in the FY2026 national budget, that is 16.5%.[7] Japan’s calculator page (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/jp/) lets you try other amounts.

The United States: $91 a month, about $379 billion a year, 1.2% of GDP. Federal tax revenue was 10.8% of GDP in 2024, so the cost is 11.4% of it; state and local taxes are not counted.[4]

India: ₹1,800 a month, 9.2% of GDP. Central government tax revenue was 6.9% of GDP in 2022, the latest year, so the cost comes to 132% of it. India’s states raise taxes of their own, which this measure leaves out. Today’s cash schemes are far smaller; see our essay on Madhya Pradesh and cash for women (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/india-basic-income-madhya-pradesh-ladli-behna/).

Nigeria: 29,000 naira a month, 18.7% of GDP. The World Bank has no tax revenue figure for Nigeria since 2015, so it is grey on the map. Brazil: R$240 a month, 4.8% of GDP and 31% of tax revenue (2024). China: 320 yuan a month, 3.9% of GDP and 55% of central tax revenue, which was 7.0% of GDP in 2024; China’s childcare subsidy (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/china-childcare-subsidy-basic-income/) pays 3,600 yuan a year per child under 3.

The Gulf states are cheap relative to their economies: 1.1% of GDP in Qatar, 1.6% in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, 1.8% in Bahrain, 2.1% in Kuwait and 2.7% in Oman. Against tax revenue they look very different, because most of their revenue is not tax. Saudi Arabia’s tax revenue was 8.1% of GDP in 2024 but its total revenue 26.8%, so the cost is 19% of tax revenue and 5.9% of all revenue.[5] The UAE’s federal government reports tax revenue of 0.65% of GDP (2024), which puts the cost at 242% of it. Bahrain’s 2020 figure gives 63%; Qatar, Kuwait and Oman have no recent figure.

#### The big caveats

Gross, not net. These figures are the cheque, not the bill. A basic income would replace some existing benefits, and part of it would come back in tax. Neither is subtracted here.

PPP versus market prices. $3 a day at PPP is a different number of dollars at market exchange rates: about US$21 a month in India, US$12 in Syria and US$117 in Iceland and Switzerland. Where we had to use the exchange rate instead (34 places, among them Somalia and DR Congo), $3 a day means about US$90 a month, which is part of why those two top the chart.

A poverty line, not a living. $3.00 a day is the World Bank’s line for extreme poverty. In Japan it is ¥9,400 a month; the calculator’s own default for Japan is ¥30,000, and Takenaka’s proposal (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/takenaka-70000-yen-basic-income/) is ¥70,000. A basic income at ten times the poverty line costs ten times as much.

Weak tax collection. Tax revenue is not a hard limit: governments also borrow, earn from resources and state firms, and can raise taxes. But where much of the economy is informal and tax collection is weak, it is a fair sign of how much money a state can actually move. Ethiopia’s central government collected 3.4% of GDP in tax in 2024, Somalia’s 2.2%.

Central government only. The World Bank measure covers central government. Federal countries such as the United States, Germany, India, Brazil and the UAE, where states and regions also tax, look less able to pay than they are.

Old years. Ten countries’ tax figures are from 2020 and nine from 2021, while GDP is mostly for 2025; Burundi’s and the Central African Republic’s are from 2021 and DR Congo’s from 2022. We drop anything more than five years older than the GDP year, but even within that window a lot can change.

#### What it implies

For the poorest countries, a poverty-line basic income paid from their own taxes is out of reach; it would take money from outside. Transfers across borders already exist on a small scale: GiveDirectly’s study in Kenya (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-kenya) pays adults a little over $20 a month.

Partial and phased schemes cost far less. Paying only India’s children, 29% of its people, would cost 2.7% of GDP, about 39% of central tax revenue. Try other groups and amounts in the calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/).

Resource funds are another route. Alaska’s Permanent Fund (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid an annual dividend from a state fund to eligible residents since 1982.[10]

Opinion: Our read: the map does not say who will adopt a basic income. It says that for 59 countries, a floor at the extreme poverty line would cost less than a quarter of today’s tax revenue, so the obstacle there is a political choice rather than arithmetic. For 40, it cannot be paid from their own taxes alone. For more on what the evidence and the money look like, see Finland’s experiment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/), OpenResearch’s $1,000-a-month study (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/) and who would pay for a universal high income (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/).

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/india-basic-income-madhya-pradesh-ladli-behna/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/china-childcare-subsidy-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/does-cash-make-people-stop-working/

### Basic income in India: the Madhya Pradesh experiment and today’s cash for women

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/india-basic-income-madhya-pradesh-ladli-behna/
- Published: 2026-11-09

Every month about 12.5 million women in Madhya Pradesh receive Rs 1,500 in their bank accounts under the Ladli Behna scheme.[1] The state is not alone. According to PRS Legislative Research, the number of states paying largely unconditional cash to women rose from two in 2022-23 to twelve in 2025-26, and together they expect to spend Rs 1.68 trillion (Rs 1,68,040 crore) on these schemes, about 0.5% of GDP.[2]

More than a decade earlier, villages in the same state’s Indore district were the site of one of the most cited basic income pilots in the world. This essay looks at what that pilot did and found, and its limits; at what India’s 2016-17 Economic Survey said about universal basic income (UBI); and at how close today’s schemes, Ladli Behna, Ladki Bahin and PM-KISAN, come to a basic income.

#### The Madhya Pradesh pilot (2011–2013)

The pilot was run by the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) and funded by UNICEF.[3] In the larger pilot, every man, woman and child in eight villages received a monthly basic income, and their experience was compared with 12 similar “control” villages. From June 2011 to May 2012 each adult received Rs 200 a month and each child Rs 100; the amounts were then raised by 50% for inflation, to Rs 300 and Rs 150, and paid until November 2012. For families at the poverty line, that was about 30% of their spending.[3]

A smaller pilot ran in one tribal village from February 2012 to January 2013, at Rs 300 per adult and Rs 150 per child a month. 756 people received Rs 1.945 million in all, and the comparison was with another tribal village.[3] In total about 6,000 people in nine villages received a basic income. In the larger pilot 5,547 people were eligible, and the surveys covered 11,231 people in 2,034 households. The villages were chosen at random, and the survey instruments were designed by an independent economist.[3]

#### What it found

The results were published in 2015 in Basic Income: A Transformative Policy for India by Sarath Davala, Renana Jhabvala, Soumya Kapoor Mehta and Guy Standing, which is free to read online.[3] The clearest effect was on nutrition. In the basic income villages, the share of girls with a normal weight for their age rose by more than 25 percentage points, more than double the rise in control villages; for boys it rose by 14 points, against 9 in the control villages. In the tribal village, the share of children severely underweight fell from 32% to 15%.[3]

Schooling improved too: 29.0% of households receiving the basic income reported higher school attendance, against 13.5% of those not receiving it.[3] Work did not fall; it changed. The main shift was from wage labour to own-account farming and other own work, and women were the main beneficiaries of the growth in secondary economic activity.[3] Debt fell: 12.5% of households in the basic income villages reduced their debt and 5% increased it, while in the control villages only 5% reduced it and over 58% increased it.[3] Among households with a disabled member, 27% of those without the basic income saw their earnings fall, against 12% of those with it.[3]

| Area | Basic income villages | Control villages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Girls with normal weight for age | Up by more than 25 points | Less than half that |
| Boys with normal weight for age | +14 points | +9 points |
| Households reporting higher school attendance | 29.0% | 13.5% |
| Households that reduced debt | 12.5% | 5% |
| Households that increased debt | 5% | Over 58% |

#### The limits

These results need careful reading. Only 8 villages received money, with 12 for comparison; randomisation was at the village level, not the individual level. The pilot lasted about a year and a half. Most results rest on what people told surveyors. The book was written by the team behind the pilot, not by outside evaluators. The book itself reports that weight improved by 27 points in SEWA villages and by under 20 in the others, so part of the effect may come from the organisation, not only the money.[3] The authors call the evaluation a “work-in-progress”.[3] We found no independent, peer-reviewed reanalysis of the pilot.

Opinion: Still, the pilot matters for India. It tested paying every individual, every month, without conditions, and it found no sign of the fears most often raised: that people would stop working or waste the money. It is not a substitute for larger, longer, independently checked studies, but it is good early evidence. A summary is also on our timeline (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-india-mp).

#### The 2016-17 Economic Survey: “ripe for serious discussion”

Chapter 9 of the Government of India’s Economic Survey 2016-17 was devoted to UBI. It counted about 950 central schemes and sub-schemes, together about 5% of GDP in budget allocations, and found that the poorest districts often received the least money, which it called evidence of “acute misallocation”.[4] It estimated that a UBI of Rs 7,620 a year, paid to 75% of the population, would cost 4.9% of GDP.[4]

The Survey also listed the case against: money might go on conspicuous spending, people might work less, men might control the money within households, and once a scheme starts it is politically hard to stop. Its conclusion was that UBI is an idea whose time has come “perhaps not for immediate implementation but at least for serious public deliberation”.[4] Before the 2019 election the Congress party promised NYAY, Rs 72,000 a year for the poorest 20% of families.[5] That was not implemented either.

#### PM-KISAN: cash for farmers

What was implemented was PM-KISAN. Since 24 February 2019, every eligible landholding farmer family has received Rs 6,000 a year in three instalments of Rs 2,000, straight into a bank account; income tax payers, government employees and higher-income groups are excluded.[6] The 24th instalment, on 30 October 2026, paid about Rs 186.9 billion to more than 93.4 million farmers, bringing the total paid so far above Rs 4.64 trillion.[7] The 2026-27 budget estimate is Rs 635 billion.[8] It is regular and in cash, but it is paid per family and only to farmers who own land; landless farm labourers are not covered.

#### Cash for women: Ladli Behna, Ladki Bahin and other states

Madhya Pradesh’s Ladli Behna scheme was announced on 28 January 2023, ahead of that year’s state election, and first paid on 10 June 2023. It began at Rs 1,000 a month, rose to Rs 1,250 from October 2023 and to Rs 1,500 from November 2025.[9] It is for married women (including widowed, divorced and deserted women) aged 21 to under 60 whose self-declared family income is no more than Rs 250,000 a year; families with an income tax payer, a government employee or pensioner, more than five acres of land or a four-wheeler are excluded. The official portal lists 12,522,542 eligible applicants.[1] Its budget rose from Rs 186.69 billion in 2025-26 to Rs 238.83 billion in 2026-27. In October 2026 Chief Minister Mohan Yadav said: “Little did I know that becoming Chief Minister would bring such a heavy financial burden”.[9]

Maharashtra’s Majhi Ladki Bahin scheme has paid women aged 21 to 65 Rs 1,500 a month since July 2024.[10][2] The ruling Mahayuti alliance promised in its manifesto to raise it to Rs 2,100, but the 2025-26 budget did not; the allocation fell from Rs 460 billion the year before to Rs 360 billion.[10] A verification drive then removed more than 9.2 million beneficiaries from the roughly 24.3 to 24.7 million found eligible in the first phase. About 6 million women had failed to complete the mandatory e-KYC, and about 1.4 to 1.5 million had a family income above the Rs 250,000 limit. The Comptroller and Auditor General questioned Rs 35.41 billion of spending under the scheme.[11]

According to PRS, these twelve states ran such schemes in 2025-26:[2]

| State | Scheme | Rs per month | Budget 2025-26 (Rs crore) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maharashtra | Majhi Ladki Bahin | 1,500 | 36,000 |
| Karnataka | Gruha Lakshmi | 2,000 | 28,608 |
| West Bengal | Lakshmir Bhandar | 1,000–1,200 | 26,700 |
| Madhya Pradesh | Ladli Behna | 1,250 | 18,669 |
| Tamil Nadu | Magalir Urimai Thogai | 1,000 | 13,807 |
| Jharkhand | Maiyan Samman | 2,500 | 13,363 |
| Odisha | Subhadra | 833 | 10,145 |
| Chhattisgarh | Mahtari Vandan | 1,000 | 5,500 |
| Delhi | Mahila Samriddhi | 2,500 | 5,110 |
| Assam | Orunodoi | 1,250 | 5,000 |
| Haryana | Lado Laxmi | 2,100 | 5,000 |
| Himachal Pradesh | Pyari Behna | 1,500 | 138 |

These are 2025-26 budget figures (one crore is ten million); several amounts have changed since, such as Madhya Pradesh’s rise to Rs 1,500 in November 2025.[9] PRS also noted that six of the twelve states expect a revenue deficit, and that these transfers cut Madhya Pradesh’s revenue surplus from 1.1% of state GDP to 0.4%.[2]

#### Where the money goes

There are still few studies of these schemes’ effects. In a July 2026 working paper for the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM), economists at the State Bank of India used bank account data and found that Ladki Bahin raised beneficiaries’ month-end balances by about 84% (Rs 6,884) and their spending by about 46% (Rs 1,349); Odisha’s Subhadra scheme raised balances by about 45% and spending by 28%. About 90 paise of each extra rupee was spent, which the authors read as a sign of tight budgets.[12] The comparison was with women whose family income was just above the eligibility limit. These are account data: they show saving and spending, not effects on nutrition, schooling or decisions at home.

#### Is it a basic income?

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”.[14] Measured against it:

| Criterion | Madhya Pradesh pilot | Ladli Behna | PM-KISAN |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Periodic | Yes, monthly | Yes, monthly | Yes, three times a year |
| Cash | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Individual | Yes, every adult and child | Yes, into the woman’s own account | No, per farmer family |
| Universal | Everyone in the village | No, married women aged 21–60 | No, landholding farmers |
| Unconditional | Yes | Income and other conditions | Income and other conditions |

The Madhya Pradesh pilot, small as it was, was very nearly a basic income. Today’s schemes are regular and in cash, and the women’s schemes are individual, but they are not universal: they depend on income, age, marital status or land. “Targeted cash transfers” is the more accurate name.

#### What would it cost for everyone?

If Ladli Behna’s Rs 1,500 a month went to every adult in India, the basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=in&w=adults&m=1500) puts the gross cost at about Rs 18.6 lakh crore (Rs 18.6 trillion) a year, about 5.4% of GDP. For comparison, India’s nominal GDP in 2025-26 was Rs 346.36 lakh crore;[13] the states’ schemes for women together come to about 0.5% of GDP,[2] and PM-KISAN to about 0.18%.[8] The Economic Survey’s 4.9% assumed a smaller amount (Rs 7,620 a year) for 75% of people.[4] These are gross figures; they do not count savings from replacing other schemes.

#### Neither “basic income has arrived in India” nor “just election freebies”

Opinion: Ladli Behna and Ladki Bahin are not basic incomes. They are for some women, with conditions, and they were often launched or raised just before elections. When the bills grow, promised increases are postponed and lists shrink in the name of verification; not every woman who could not complete e-KYC is ineligible.

Opinion: But dismissing them as mere freebies is also wrong. The machinery to put cash into tens of millions of women’s own accounts every month now exists, and account data show the money is mostly spent and saved. The Madhya Pradesh pilot showed that unconditional cash for every individual can turn into better nutrition, schooling and work.

Opinion: The question is whether these schemes can move beyond the election cycle towards a stable, legally grounded and honestly evaluated income floor. That needs three things: sustainable funding, fewer and clearer conditions, and independent evaluation. The state that ran the experiment in 2011 also has the best chance to take that step.

### China’s 3,600-yuan childcare subsidy: who gets it, and is it a basic income?

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/china-childcare-subsidy-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-09

On 28 July 2025, the general offices of China’s Communist Party Central Committee and State Council issued an implementation plan for a national childcare subsidy. From 1 January 2025, every child under 3 qualifies, and the national base rate is 3,600 yuan per child per year, or 300 yuan a month.[1] Zhu Kun of the Chinese Academy of Fiscal Sciences told the People’s Daily it was “the first universal cash subsidy our country has paid to residents”.[4]

No income test, no distinction between first and third children, cash straight to families: it sounds a lot like what people mean by a basic income. Is it? This essay first sets out the rules: who qualifies, how to claim, who pays and how much has actually been paid. Then it looks at the birth figures behind the policy and at research on whether cash raises births. Finally it measures the subsidy against the definition of basic income, and compares it with Hong Kong’s HK$10,000 payout in 2020.

#### Who gets it, and how much

The subsidy covers children under 3 “born in accordance with laws and regulations”, until they turn 3.[1] First, second and third children all qualify, and there is no income threshold.[2] Children born before 2025 who were still under 3 in 2025 receive a pro-rated amount for the months left. Xinhua’s example: a child born in December 2023 can receive 24 months, 7,200 yuan in total.[2] A child born in 2025 or later can receive up to about 10,800 yuan from birth to age 3.

One parent or another guardian applies in the place where the child’s household registration (hukou) is held.[1] Most claims go through a national online system reached via Alipay, WeChat and provincial government service platforms; claims can also be made in person at the township or street office. The National Health Commission declared applications “fully open” nationwide on 8 September 2025.[7]

It is not automatic. Rules from the National Health Commission and the Ministry of Finance say the first claim must be made in the year of birth or the year after, followed by a renewal in each of the next two years; a claim not filed in time “is deemed to have given up eligibility for that year”.[5] The subsidy is “calculated by year and paid once a year as a lump sum” into the claimant’s or child’s bank or social security card account, with provinces paying out at least one batch each quarter.[5][1] Claims for 2026 opened on 5 January 2026, with a new renewal function.[8] For children born in 2022 to 2024, the deadline for a first claim has been extended from the end of 2025 to 31 December 2026.[11]

Two easily missed rules matter. The subsidy is exempt from individual income tax.[6] And when eligibility for minimum living allowance (dibao) or extreme-hardship support is assessed, the subsidy is not counted as household or personal income.[1] The poorest families do not lose their dibao by receiving it.

| Item | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Who | Children under 3; first, second and third children alike[1][2] |
| Amount | National base rate 3,600 yuan per child per year; local governments may pay more[1] |
| Income test | None[2] |
| Where to claim | The child’s place of household registration, online or in person[1][7] |
| How it is paid | Once a year as a lump sum, into a bank or social security card account[5] |
| Tax | Exempt from individual income tax[6] |
| Minimum living allowance | Not counted as household or personal income[1] |
| Claim needed? | Yes, every year; a missed year is forfeited[5] |

#### Who pays, and how much has been paid

The central government covers part of the cost of the base rate for eastern, central and western regions in different proportions; at a State Council press conference officials said “the centre bears about 90% overall”, with an initial 2025 budget of about 90 billion yuan.[1][3] If a local government pays more than the base rate, it funds the extra itself.[1]

Here is what has happened in practice. By 31 December 2025 all 31 provinces had started paying, more than 24 million children had been paid, and the payout rate for 2025 was about 80%.[10] The Ministry of Finance said at the end of January 2026 that governments at all levels had set aside about 100 billion yuan for 2025, and that more than 30 million children had been paid.[9] The 2026 Government Work Report lists “fully implementing the childcare subsidy, benefiting more than 30 million infants” among the previous year’s achievements.[12] For 2026 the central government has allocated 99.9 billion yuan, up 10.6%, and total spending at all levels is expected to be about 110 billion yuan.[10] By 21 July 2026, 27.51 million claims for 2026 had been filed, 27.13 million approved and 25.16 million children paid.[11]

Compared with the economy, it is small. China’s GDP in 2025 was 140.19 trillion yuan.[13] About 100 billion yuan is about 0.07% of GDP; about 110 billion in 2026 is about 0.08%. Compared with household incomes it is not small: 3,600 yuan a year is about 8% of 2025 per-capita disposable income nationally (43,377 yuan), 15% for rural residents (24,456 yuan) and 6% for urban residents (56,502 yuan).[13] For a rural family, it is real money.

Opinion: We found no announcement raising the 3,600-yuan base rate in 2026, and no national evaluation of the subsidy’s effects. How much has been paid is well documented. Whether it has changed family budgets or decisions about children is not yet known.

#### Why now: births

The background is a fast fall in births. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, 9.54 million babies were born in China in 2024, a birth rate of 6.77 per thousand.[14] In 2025 births fell to 7.92 million, a rate of 5.63 per thousand, while 11.31 million people died; the population at the end of the year was 1.40489 billion, 3.39 million fewer than a year earlier.[13] Births fell by about 17% in one year.

Note that most babies born in 2025 were conceived in 2024, and the national plan was published only in July 2025. The 2025 figures cannot be used to judge the subsidy. The figures for 2026 and later may start to tell us something. Alongside the subsidy, a policy of free education in the final year of preschool reached 14 million children in 2025.[12]

#### Cities went first: Hohhot, Tianmen, Panzhihua

Before the national plan, some cities tried more generous payments. Panzhihua in Sichuan announced in July 2021 that it would pay 500 yuan a month for each second or third child until age 3.[17] From 1 March 2025, Hohhot in Inner Mongolia paid 10,000 yuan once for a first child; 50,000 yuan for a second child, at 10,000 a year until age 5; and 100,000 yuan for a third or later child, at 10,000 a year until age 10. About 20,000 babies were born in Hohhot in 2023.[15] Tianmen in Hubei pays 2,300 yuan once and then 800 yuan a month until age 3 for a second child, and 3,300 yuan once and then 1,000 yuan a month for a third.[16]

Did these payments raise births? The evidence is thin. China News Service reported that births in Tianmen rose 17% in 2024, the first rise in eight years, but gave no statistical source and could not separate the subsidy from other factors.[16] An official in Hohhot said births had already edged up in 2024, before the new subsidy began.[15] The local figures are worth watching, but they are not causal evidence.

#### Can cash raise births?

International research suggests some effect, usually modest and not cheap. The most cited study is from Quebec. The economist Kevin Milligan studied the province’s policy of paying families up to C$8,000 for a new child. Comparing groups by time, place and family type, at both the start and the end of the policy, he found “a strong effect of the policy on fertility”.[18] But that was a payment tied to a birth, not a steady 300 yuan a month.

South Korea is a reminder in the other direction. According to its Board of Audit and Inspection, the country spent 380.2 trillion won on low fertility from 2006 to 2020.[19] Its total fertility rate still fell to a world-low 0.72 in 2023, before recovering to 0.75 in 2024 and 0.80 in 2025. Officials put the recovery down mainly to more marriages (up 8.1% in 2025) and a larger number of people in their thirties, not to any one payment.[20]

Opinion: Our reading of the research: cash can bring some births forward or tip some families towards another child, but cash alone rarely reverses a long fall in fertility; housing, schooling, jobs and time for care matter as much. On the other hand, the effect of cash for families with children on child poverty is clear. In our essay on refundable tax credits (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/refundable-tax-credit-vs-basic-income/) we saw US child poverty fall sharply when the Child Tax Credit was expanded in 2021 and rise again when the expansion ended. So the subsidy should not be judged only on whether it raises the number of births.

#### Is it a basic income? BIEN’s five criteria

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”.[21] We used this yardstick in our essay on Japan’s ¥100,000 payment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/). Applied to the childcare subsidy:

| Criterion | Childcare subsidy | Basic income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Periodic | Yes, once a year | Yes |
| Cash | Yes, into a bank or card account | Yes |
| Individual | Counted per child, claimed by a parent or guardian | Each person receives their own |
| Universal | No, only children under 3 | Everyone |
| Unconditional | No income or work test, but must be claimed each year | Unconditional |

So the subsidy meets “periodic” and “cash”, largely meets “unconditional”, partly meets “individual”, and does not meet “universal”. A more accurate description is a cash payment for young children without an income test: an early version of what many countries call a child benefit or child allowance. The biggest difference from a basic income is that it covers only the first three years of life.

#### Hong Kong’s HK$10,000 in 2020

In the Chinese-speaking world, payments to everyone are rare; one example is Hong Kong’s Cash Payout Scheme of 2020. The budget of 26 February 2020 announced HK$10,000 for every Hong Kong permanent resident aged 18 or over, expected to reach about 7 million people at a cost of about HK$71 billion.[22] Banks began taking online registrations on 21 June 2020; the money went into bank accounts, or could be collected as a cheque through Hongkong Post.[23]

In January 2021 the government told the Legislative Council that by 21 January about HK$64 billion had been paid to some 6.4 million people, more than 90% of those eligible, and that administration had cost about HK$306 million. On the effect, it said only that it “believed” the money “should have certain stimulating effect on consumption”; it gave no measurement.[24] By 23 November 2021 more than 6.5 million eligible registrants had been paid.[25]

Opinion: Hong Kong’s scheme was universal, reaching almost every adult permanent resident, but it was paid once. China’s subsidy is periodic, but only for children under 3. A basic income needs both: paid to everyone, and paid again and again. Japan’s ¥100,000 in 2020 was also one-off, and as we found (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/), much of it was saved.

#### What would a floor for everyone cost?

What if 300 yuan a month went to everyone? With the basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=cn&w=all&m=300), 300 yuan a month for every person in China comes to about 5.1 trillion yuan a year gross, about 3.6% of GDP. For all children under 18 only, it is about 970 billion yuan a year, about 0.7% of GDP, roughly nine times the current subsidy. These are gross amounts, not net costs, and they do not count other spending that might be replaced.

For comparison, since 1982 the US state of Alaska has paid an annual dividend from a state fund to eligible residents of every age. It is the longest-running scheme close to a basic income; see it on our timeline (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska).

#### Neither “basic income has arrived” nor “a drop in the ocean”

Opinion: The childcare subsidy is not a basic income. It covers only the first three years of life, it is worth about 15% of rural per-capita disposable income, and it must be claimed every year. Calling it “China’s basic income” is an overstatement.

Opinion: Nor can it be waved away as a drop in the ocean. For the first time, China pays cash nationwide to every family with a young child, without an income test: more than 30 million children in a year, tax-free, and without costing anyone their minimum living allowance. Those are the hardest practical parts of any basic income: finding everyone, getting money into accounts, and making sure the poorest do not lose other support by taking it. China has now built such a system for children under 3.

Opinion: Three things are worth watching: whether the rate rises with incomes and prices, whether the age limit is extended, and whether births and child poverty change from 2026 on. If the payment one day covers more ages, it will come ever closer to a child basic income.

16. China News Service — Cash subsidies, childcare vouchers: localities explore birth subsidies (15 Aug 2025, in Chinese): https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2025/08-15/10465048.shtml
17. The Beijing News — Panzhihua to pay 500 yuan a month per child in childcare subsidy (30 Jul 2021, in Chinese): https://www.bjnews.com.cn/detail/162764311414398.html
18. NBER — Kevin Milligan, Subsidizing the Stork: New Evidence on Tax Incentives and Fertility, Working Paper 8845 (2002; Review of Economics and Statistics, 2005): https://www.nber.org/papers/w8845
19. Asia Business Daily — 380.2 trillion won spent on low fertility from 2006 to 2020, Board of Audit and Inspection (13 Aug 2021): https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2021081313594120510
